title: Through Both Doors at Once: How Waves Add Up, and Why Single Particles Still Make Stripes

intro.summary: These four sources ask what happens when waves meet, and what that tells us about light and matter. The Wikipedia article 'Wave interference' and a LibreTexts physics chapter explain superposition: overlapping waves add point by point, so they can reinforce or cancel. The Wikipedia article 'Double-slit experiment' and a LibreTexts chemistry chapter show the same arithmetic behind the bright and dark stripes behind two slits. They then report the surprise: electrons and photons sent one at a time still build up the striped pattern, and the stripes vanish when detectors record which slit each particle used. The main limit is that these are encyclopedia and textbook summaries, not one original study. They also say plainly that what the results mean is still disputed: Copenhagen, many-worlds, de Broglie–Bohm and relational readings all predict the same observations but tell different stories about them. This lesson does not cover standing waves, beats, coherence requirements, the single-slit diffraction envelope, quantum erasers or the interpretations in depth; each would make a good follow-up.
background: A wave is a disturbance that travels, like a ripple on a pond or a vibration in the air, while the water or air itself mostly stays in place.
The highest point of a wave is a crest, the lowest point is a trough, and the height of a crest above the resting level is the wave's amplitude.
The distance from one crest to the next is the wavelength, and for light we see wavelength as colour.
We only ever see how bright light is at a spot. Brightness, called intensity, goes with the square of the wave's height, not the height itself.
intro.aha: Electrons fired one at a time each land as a single dot, yet thousands of them build up stripes that only make sense if each one went through both slits, and the stripes vanish the moment you check which slit it used.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: Drop two stones in a pond and the ripples cross, building up in some places and flattening out in others. Physicists asked whether light, and even tiny bits of matter like electrons, behave the same way. The test is simple: shine something through two narrow slits and look at what lands on a screen behind them. If light were a spray of tiny pellets, you would expect two bright strips. If it is a wave, you would expect something stranger.
primer.quote: In modern physics, the double-slit experiment demonstrates that light and matter can exhibit behavior associated with both classical particles and classical waves.

primer.heading: What was done
primer.body: The rule behind all of this is superposition: where waves overlap, their heights simply add, and a trough counts as a negative height. Thomas Young described a two-slit demonstration with light around 1801–1803, though historians question whether he ran exactly the two-slit version. From 1927 on, others showed that electrons behave the same way, and later atoms and large molecules did too. Experimenters then dimmed the source until particles went through one at a time, and some placed detectors at the slits to find out which slit each particle used.
primer.quote: The principle of superposition of waves states that when two or more propagating waves of the same type are incident on the same point, the resultant amplitude at that point is equal to the vector sum of the amplitudes of the individual waves.

primer.heading: What was found
primer.body: With two slits open, the screen shows many alternating bright and dark stripes, not two strips. The dark stripes are places where the waves from the two slits arrive crest-to-trough and cancel. The surprise comes when particles are sent one at a time. Each one lands as a single dot, yet after thousands of dots the same stripes appear.
primer.quote: The resulting pattern on the screen is the same as if each individual particle had passed through both slits.

primer.heading: The twist: looking changes the result
primer.body: If you place detectors at the slits to learn which slit each particle took, the stripes disappear. The screen then shows just the two single-slit patterns added together. Later experiments found the change can be gradual: partial path information gives fainter stripes rather than none.
primer.quote: A well-known thought experiment predicts that if particle detectors are positioned at the slits, showing through which slit a photon goes, the interference pattern will disappear.
primer.quote_where: "Which-way" experiments and the principle of complementarity

primer.heading: Why it matters, and its limits
primer.body: Feynman called this experiment the heart of quantum mechanics, and the same interference ideas run telescopes, length standards and soap-bubble colours. Everyone agrees on the measurements and the maths. People disagree about what the maths says is really happening. Some say the question 'which slit?' has no answer until you measure. Others say each particle takes one slit but is guided by a wave that goes through both. Others again say reality branches. These sources do not settle that dispute, and neither does this lesson.
primer.quote: The interpretation of quantum mechanics is still an unsolved problem in modern physics

concepts.title: Where waves meet, their heights add
concepts.idea: When two waves overlap, the height at each point is just the sum of the two waves' heights there, with troughs counting as negative.

predict.question: Two ripples cross on a pond. At one spot, at one instant, ripple A on its own would lift the water 3 cm above calm. Ripple B on its own would lower it 5 cm below calm. Where is the water surface at that spot?
options: 2 cm below the calm level
8 cm above the calm level
8 cm below the calm level
Exactly at the calm level, because a high and a low always cancel
You can't tell, because one ripple blocks the other
why: Right: the rise counts as +3 and the dip counts as −5, so the surface sits at +3 + (−5) = −2, which is 2 cm below calm.
This adds the sizes and forgets the signs. A dip is a negative height, so it pulls the total down instead of adding to it.
This treats both pushes as downward. Ripple A lifts the water, so its +3 partly offsets B's −5.
A high and a low cancel completely only when they are the same size. Here the dip is bigger, so 2 cm of dip is left over.
Overlapping waves don't block each other. Each one adds its own height at the spot, so the sum is simply +3 − 5.

terms.means: The rule that where waves overlap, their heights simply add at each point
How far the surface is pushed from its calm level at a point: up counts as plus, down counts as minus
The highest point of a wave, where its height is most positive
The lowest point of a wave, where its height is most negative

model.title: Two waves and the surface they make together
model.note: Teaching model: two smooth waves frozen at one instant along a single line. Wave 2 has half the wavelength of wave 1, so their high and low points fall in different places. Real ripples move, spread out and lose height. Heights are in arbitrary units. Numbers are illustrative, not data from the sources.

steps.say: This picture freezes waves along a line, like a photo of ripples on a pond. The flat line is calm water.
This curve is wave 1. Its slider sets how tall it is.
This curve is wave 2, a shorter, choppier wave. It has its own height slider.
This solid curve shows the water when both waves are there at once.
The upright line is a check spot. Slide it along the water to inspect any point.
These boxes read off each wave's height, and the combined height, right at the check spot.

explore.prompt: Slide the check spot and change the heights. Hunt for places where the two waves fight each other.

goals.text: Find a spot where wave 1 is clearly above calm, yet the two waves together leave the water almost exactly at calm level.
hints: If wave 1 is up, what must wave 2 be doing there for the total to be zero?
Look in the left part of the picture, where wave 1 is still above calm but wave 2 has already dipped below it.
Slide the check spot between wave 1's highest point and where wave 1 next crosses the calm line. Watch the combined box shrink toward zero.

goals.text: Make the water sit clearly below calm level at a spot where wave 1 is pushing it up.
hints: A negative height can outweigh a positive one.
First find a spot where wave 1 is up only a little and wave 2 is down.
Then make wave 2 taller, so its dip outweighs wave 1's rise at that spot.

feedback.correct: Yes. The rise counts as plus and the dip counts as minus, so +3 + (−5) = −2. The water sits 2 cm below calm.
feedback.incorrect: The rule is plain addition with signs. A dip is a negative height, so it subtracts. Equal sizes would cancel exactly, but here the dip is bigger, so the surface ends up 2 cm below calm.

steps.say: Both waves have height 1, and the check spot is near the left. Wave 1 lifts the water 0.84 here and wave 2 lifts it 0.91. The combined height is 1.75, which is just 0.84 + 0.91.
This adding at every point is called superposition. The water doesn't pick one wave. Each wave pushes the surface, and the pushes add up.

How far the surface is pushed from calm is its displacement. Up counts as plus, down counts as minus. Here wave 1 is at its highest point, its crest: 1.00. Wave 2 is near calm at −0.06, so the total is 0.94.
Slide on. Wave 1 is now at a low point, a trough, with height −0.87. Wave 2 is near its crest at +0.85. Add them: about −0.02. The surface is almost calm, because a rise and an equal dip cancel.
Here both waves are in troughs: −0.71 and −1.00. Two negatives add to a deeper dip of −1.71.
Shrink wave 2 to nothing. The combined curve now lies exactly on wave 1, because adding zero changes nothing.

Now give both waves real height. The combined curve looks lumpy, like neither wave on its own. Yet at the check spot it is still simply −1.06 + (−1.20) = −2.26. Every point of that strange shape is one sum.

understand.explanation: When two waves overlap, the surface at each spot is pushed by both at once, and the pushes simply add. A rise counts as plus and a dip counts as minus. So a crest on a crest makes a taller bump, and a crest on an equal trough leaves the surface calm there. Neither wave blocks or bends the other: each one adds its own height. The sources illustrate this with two stones dropped in a pond, whose ripples add point by point, and with drawings of identical and non-identical waves added together. The textbook adds that most complicated-looking waves are really sums of simple ones. One caveat: plain adding applies when the pushes are along the same line. For light, the field cannot be watched adding directly, so superposition there is an assumed rule that explains what we see.
understand.quote: When the two waves overlap, the net displacement at a particular point is the sum of the displacements of the individual waves.

connect.caption: This is the model's rule. It is the superposition principle that the sources state in words; the wave-interference article writes the sum of two waves as W₁ + W₂. W₁ is wave 1's height at the check spot and W₂ is wave 2's. Their sum is the combined height, with dips entering as negative numbers.

concepts.recap: Where waves overlap, just add their heights point by point: rises are plus, dips are minus.

concepts.title: In step they grow, out of step they cancel
concepts.idea: Shifting one wave relative to the other changes the combined height from double (crest on crest) down to zero (crest on trough), following 2A·cos(φ/2).

predict.question: Picture sliding wave 2 by a whole cycle (360°). That is further than this slider goes. With both heights equal, what does the combined wave look like?
options: Twice as tall as one wave, the same as with no shift at all
Completely flat: the two waves cancel
Exactly as tall as one wave
Some leftover in-between height, because the shift is so large
why: Correct. After a whole cycle, every crest of wave 2 lands on the next crest of wave 1. So the waves line up exactly as they did at 0°, and the heights add to double. In the rule, cos(360°/2) = cos(180°) = −1, and the size 2A·|−1| is 2A.
Cancelling needs crest on trough, which happens at half a cycle (180°). It happens again at 540°, but not at 360°. A whole cycle puts crest back on crest.
One wave's height came out at a 120° shift. A whole cycle is three times that shift and brings the waves fully back into line.
A bigger shift is not a bigger effect. The pattern repeats every cycle, so only the leftover part of a cycle matters, and a whole cycle leaves nothing over.

terms.means: How far one wave is slid along relative to the other, measured as a share of one cycle: a whole cycle is 360° (or 2π), half a cycle is 180° (or π)
Waves meeting crest on crest, so their heights add up to a bigger wave
Waves meeting crest on trough, so their heights work against each other and the combined wave shrinks, down to zero if they are equal

model.title: Two waves and the surface they make together
model.note: Teaching model: two smooth waves frozen at one instant along a single line. Unlike the previous picture, wave 2 now has the same wavelength as wave 1, because the rule here only holds for waves of the same frequency. A new slider slides wave 2 sideways. Real waves move, spread out and lose height. Heights are in arbitrary units. The 'tallest point' uses the general formula for two heights, which becomes the sources' 2A·cos(φ/2) when the heights are equal. Numbers are illustrative, not data from the sources.

outputs.label: Tallest point of both together
outputs.expr: sqrt(max(0, a1 * a1 + a2 * a2 + 2 * a1 * a2 * cos(shift * pi / 180)))

series.label: Both together
series.expr: a1 * sin(x) + a2 * sin(x + shift * pi / 180)

hlines.y: sqrt(max(0, a1 * a1 + a2 * a2 + 2 * a1 * a2 * cos(shift * pi / 180)))
hlines.label: Tallest point

points.y: a1 * sin(p) + a2 * sin(p + shift * pi / 180)
points.label: Together

steps.say: This is the same picture as before: two dashed waves, and the solid curve where their heights add. One change: wave 2 now has the same spacing between crests as wave 1.
This new slider slides wave 2 sideways along the line, without changing its height or spacing. Watch the dashed wave 2 move.
This box and the line it draws give the tallest point the solid curve reaches. Keep an eye on them as wave 2 slides.

explore.prompt: Slide wave 2 and steer the solid curve. Make it vanish, then find the in-between shift where two waves together are only as tall as one.

goals.text: Make the solid 'Both together' curve lie flat on the calm level everywhere, with both waves still at a real height
hints: For the two waves to cancel everywhere, what must sit under every crest of wave 1?
Slide wave 2 until its troughs line up exactly under wave 1's crests, and watch the 'Tallest point' box drop.
The right shift is between 150° and 210°.

goals.text: Keep both heights where they start, and make the two waves together reach exactly as high as one wave alone
hints: The combined height falls smoothly from double to zero as you slide, so it must pass through the height of one wave somewhere in between.
Start from the flat setting and slide back toward 'in step', watching the 'Tallest point' box climb.
The right shift is between 90° and 150°.

feedback.correct: Yes. Sliding a wave by a whole cycle brings every crest onto the next crest, so the waves line up as if nothing had moved and the heights double. Only the part of a cycle left over matters.
feedback.incorrect: It is tempting to think a bigger shift means more cancelling. But the waves repeat, so the effect repeats too: double at 0°, zero at 180°, double again at 360°. A whole cycle puts crest back on crest.

steps.say: Start with no shift. Every crest of wave 2 sits right on a crest of wave 1, and every trough on a trough. The heights add, so the solid curve is twice as tall: the tallest point reads 2.
How far one wave is slid along the other is called the phase difference. Crest-on-crest growth at zero phase difference is called constructive interference.
Slide wave 2 a quarter of a cycle, to 90°. Crests now land partly on slopes. The sum is still a wave of the same spacing, but shorter: about 1.41 tall.
Slide further, to 135°. The crests are getting close to the troughs, and the solid curve keeps shrinking: about 0.77.

At 180°, half a cycle, every crest of one wave meets a trough of the other. Look at the check spot: wave 1 is at +1, wave 2 at −1, together 0. The same holds at every spot, so the solid curve is flat. This is destructive interference.
Cancelling is only complete when the heights match. Shrink wave 2 to half height and the crests are no longer fully filled in. What is left is the difference between the two heights, 0.5.

Make them equal again and the surface goes perfectly calm: two real waves, adding up to nothing. For equal waves the size of the sum follows 2A·cos(shift/2). That gives 2A at 0°, falling smoothly to 0 at 180°.

understand.explanation: When two waves with the same spacing overlap, what decides the result is how far one is slid along the other: the phase difference. With no shift, crest meets crest and the heights add to double (constructive interference). At half a cycle (180°, or π), crest meets trough and they cancel to zero if their heights are equal (destructive interference). If the heights differ, what is left is the difference. In between, the combined height shrinks smoothly, following 2A·cos(φ/2). The sources show this by adding two cosine waves with a trigonometric identity, not by measuring. They also note that pure doubling or pure cancelling needs precisely aligned identical waves; most real waves land somewhere in between.
understand.quote: Constructive interference occurs when the phase difference between the waves is an even multiple of π (180°), whereas destructive interference occurs when the difference is an odd multiple of π. If the difference between the phases is intermediate between these two extremes, then the magnitude of the displacement of the summed waves lies between the minimum and maximum values.

connect.caption: This is the sources' sum of two equal waves. A is the height of each wave (the wave 1 slider, with wave 2 set equal to it). φ is the shift slider: 180° is π, and 360° is 2π. The front part, 2A·cos(φ/2), sets how tall the combined wave is; the 'Tallest point' box shows its size. The last cosine says the sum is still a wave with the same spacing.

activities.prompt: Look at the two extremes side by side. Same two waves, same heights; only the shift differs.

cases.label: Half a cycle: crest on trough

activities.takeaway: Nothing about either wave changed except where its crests sit. That alone takes the combined wave from double height to nothing.

concepts.recap: Line crests up and two waves make one twice as tall. Slide one by half a cycle and equal waves cancel to nothing. Shifts in between give in-between heights, following 2A·cos(φ/2).

concepts.title: Two slits paint a row of stripes
concepts.idea: Light from the two slits travels different distances to each spot on the screen, so the spots alternate between in step (bright) and out of step (dark), giving stripes spaced by w = zλ/d.

predict.question: A lab swaps its 0.5 μm green laser for a 0.7 μm red one, but needs the stripes on the screen to stay exactly as far apart as before. Which single change does that?
options: Move the slits farther apart, by the same factor the wavelength grew (0.5 mm → 0.7 mm)
Move the slits closer together
Move the screen farther away
Nothing: the colour of the light does not change the stripe spacing
why: Right. Longer waves need more extra trip per whole wavelength, so the stripes spread by 0.7/0.5. A wider gap squeezes them back by the same factor. A closer screen would also work.
Tempting if you think 'closer slits, tighter pattern'. But a smaller gap makes the extra trip grow more slowly, so the stripes spread even further. The gap sits underneath in w = zλ/d.
A farther screen lets the same angles spread over more distance, so the stripes widen. Redder light already widened them, so this makes the mismatch worse.
Colour is wavelength, and wavelength sets how much extra trip makes one whole wave. Longer waves put the in-step spots farther apart, so the spacing does change.

terms.means: How much farther the light from one slit travels than the light from the other to reach the same spot
One bright (or dark) stripe in the pattern on the screen
The distance from one bright stripe to the next, written w

model.title: Brightness across a screen lit through two slits
model.note: Teaching model: it assumes very narrow slits, a single-colour laser and a screen far away compared with the slit gap, so the brightness follows cos²(π·d·y / (λ·z)). It ignores the slow fading of the stripes away from the centre caused by each slit's own spreading, and it shows brightness as a share of the brightest spot. The spacing rule w = zλ/d and the example (0.5 mm gap, 0.6 μm light, 1 m away, giving 1.2 mm) come from source s3. Other settings are illustrative.

outputs.label: Extra trip at the spot (in wavelengths)

x.label: Position on the screen, from the centre (mm)

steps.say: One laser shines through two narrow slits onto a screen. This curve is how bright the screen is at each position: peaks are bright, dips are dark.
This slider sets the light's wavelength, which is its colour. Watch the stripes respond.
This one sets the gap between the two slits.
This one sets how far away the screen is.
The vertical line marks one spot on the screen. These boxes tell you how much farther one slit's light travels to reach it, and how bright it is there.

explore.prompt: Now play with the stripes yourself: stretch the pattern, then hunt down a dark stripe by thinking about the extra trip.

goals.text: Make the stripes exactly twice as far apart as in the source's example (which gives 1.2 mm)
hints: Which settings appear in the spacing rule, and which ones widen the stripes?
The slit gap sits underneath in the rule, so shrinking it spreads the stripes. The screen distance sits on top, so it works the other way.
To double the spacing, change just one setting by a factor of two in the right direction.

goals.text: Park the marked spot on the second dark stripe to the right of the centre
hints: Dark stripes appear where one slit's light travels an odd number of half wavelengths farther.
The first dark stripe needs half a wavelength of extra trip. The second needs three halves. Watch the 'Extra trip' box as you slide the spot.
The second dark stripe sits one and a half stripe spacings from the centre.

feedback.correct: Yes. The spacing is w = zλ/d, so a longer wavelength spreads the stripes. Widening the slit gap by the same factor (or bringing the screen closer by it) cancels that out exactly.
feedback.incorrect: The spacing follows w = zλ/d. Redder light means a bigger λ, which spreads the stripes. To undo that you need something that squeezes them by the same factor: a wider slit gap d, or a closer screen z.

steps.say: Start with the source's own setup: a 0.5 mm slit gap, 0.6 μm light, and a screen 1 m away. At the centre both slits are equally far, so their waves arrive in step. The extra trip is 0 and the spot is fully bright.

Slide the spot 0.6 mm to the right. Light from the far slit now travels half a wavelength more. This extra distance is called the path difference. Crest meets trough, so the waves cancel and the screen goes dark.
At 1.2 mm the path difference is a whole wavelength. Crest meets crest again, so the spot is bright. Each bright band like this is called a fringe.
The distance from one bright fringe to the next is the fringe spacing, w. Here it is 1.2 mm, matching the source's worked example.
Now double the slit gap. The path difference grows twice as fast as you move along the screen, so a whole wavelength is reached in half the distance. The fringes squeeze to 0.6 mm apart.
Next, move the screen twice as far away. The same angles now spread over twice the distance, so the fringes widen back to 1.2 mm.

Put the spot at 0.6 mm: half a wavelength of path difference again, so it is dark. The whole pattern follows one rule: a wider gap squeezes the stripes, a farther screen spreads them, and longer waves spread them too. That rule is w = zλ/d.

understand.explanation: Each spot on the screen gets light from both slits, but one slit is usually a little farther away. That extra distance is the path difference. When it is a whole number of wavelengths, the two waves arrive in step and add up to a bright fringe. When it is half a wavelength, one and a half, and so on, they cancel and the spot is dark. Moving along the screen steadily increases the path difference, so bright and dark alternate at a regular spacing w = zλ/d. The source works this out for a far-away screen and checks it with an example: 0.5 mm slits and 0.6 μm light give stripes 1.2 mm apart, 1 m away. This simple rule assumes very narrow slits and a single colour. With wider slits, each slit's own spreading also dims the stripes away from the centre. Historians also question whether Thomas Young, who first described the experiment in 1801, actually performed a double-slit version.
understand.quote: When the two waves are in phase, i.e. the path difference is equal to an integral number of wavelengths, the summed amplitude, and therefore the summed intensity is maximum, and when they are in anti-phase, i.e. the path difference is equal to half a wavelength, one and a half wavelengths, etc., then the two waves cancel and the summed intensity is zero.

connect.caption: The source's fringe-spacing formula. w (stripe spacing) is the distance between bright fringes. z is the distance to the screen, λ is the wavelength, and d is the slit gap. Bigger z or λ spreads the stripes; a bigger d squeezes them. With z in metres, λ in micrometres and d in millimetres, w comes out in millimetres, as in the model.

concepts.recap: Each spot's brightness depends on how much farther one slit's light travels: whole wavelengths give bright stripes, half wavelengths give dark ones, and the stripes sit w = zλ/d apart.

activities.title: The source's own example: how far apart are the stripes?

steps.text: Write down the setup from the source: slits d = 0.5 mm apart, laser wavelength λ = 0.6 μm, screen z = 1 m away.
Put everything in metres: d = 0.0005 m and λ = 0.0000006 m.
Find the angle between neighbouring bright stripes. It is about λ/d, measured in radians (a tiny angle).
Multiply by the distance to the screen to turn that angle into a distance on the screen: w = z × λ/d.

steps.result: w = 1.2 mm, the value the source reports

activities.takeaway: Stripes about a millimetre apart, from waves less than a thousandth of a millimetre long: the far screen magnifies the tiny path differences into a pattern you can see.

concepts.title: One dot at a time, the stripes still appear
concepts.idea: Each particle lands as a single dot at a random spot, but the chance of landing at each spot follows the wave's brightness pattern, so the stripes appear only as dots pile up.

predict.question: After 3,000 particles the middle bright stripe has 493 dots. The other two bright stripes have 506 and 499. Where could particle 3,001 land, and where is it most likely to land?
options: Anywhere except the dark gaps; each bright stripe is equally likely, whatever the tally so far
Most likely the middle stripe, because it is behind and needs to catch up
In a dark gap, because the gaps have waited longest for a dot
Only in the fullest stripe, because dots attract more dots
why: Right. Each particle's chances come only from the brightness pattern. Bright stripes are equally likely, in-between spots are half as likely, and dark gaps are impossible. Earlier dots change nothing.
This feels fair, like a tally that must even out. But a particle has no record of earlier dots. The gap of a few dots is random scatter, and the next dot is no more likely to fill it.
Waiting does not raise the chance. A dark gap is where the waves from the two slits cancel, so its chance stays zero however many particles have passed.
Dots do not pull on each other. A slightly taller bar is random scatter, and the next particle's chances are set by the brightness pattern alone.

terms.means: How the chance of a particle landing is spread across the screen: high at bright stripes, half in between, zero in the dark gaps
Light and matter arrive as single dots, like particles, yet where they land follows a wave's interference pattern

model.title: Dots piling up on the screen behind two slits
model.note: Teaching model: the screen is cut into 13 spots, each a quarter of a stripe apart. Each spot's chance follows the two-slit brightness cos²(π d sinθ/λ) from the stripes lesson. The slow dimming of outer stripes caused by slit width is left out, and dark spots are treated as perfectly dark. The run grows in fixed stages, roughly tripling each time. The dot counts are one made-up random run, not data from any experiment.

outputs.label: Chance the next dot lands at this spot
Dots at this spot so far

steps.say: This is the screen behind two slits, cut into 13 spots. Each bar counts the dots that have landed in one spot.
Particles are sent through one at a time. This slider runs the experiment longer. Right now just one particle has arrived.
Ten particles, ten dots, scattered about.
This slider picks one spot to watch. Its bar changes colour.
These boxes show that spot's dots so far and the chance the next particle lands there.
Back to the start. Let's watch a run.

explore.prompt: Grow the run and watch how scattered dots turn into stripes. Then use the spot slider to see how each spot's chance shapes its pile of dots.

goals.text: Find the shortest run in which every bright spot has more dots than every in-between spot.
hints: Compare the box for the emptiest bright spot with the box for the fullest in-between spot.
At thirty particles the two were still level, so you need a longer run.
Step forward from thirty one stage at a time. Stop the first time the bright box is ahead.

goals.text: Pick a spot where the next dot is half as likely as at the middle. Then run long enough that its pile settles near half the middle's pile.
hints: A spot that is neither a bright stripe nor a dark gap has a middle-sized chance.
Move the spot slider and watch the chance box. Look for half the middle's chance.
Now push the run far enough that the random scatter is small next to the bar heights.

feedback.correct: Right. Each particle carries no memory of earlier dots. Its chances are set by the brightness pattern alone. Every bright stripe is equally likely, in-between spots are half as likely, and the dark gaps are impossible.
feedback.incorrect: It is tempting to think the screen evens itself out, but each particle lands on its own. The small differences between tallies are random scatter. The next dot's chances come only from the brightness pattern, never from the dots already there.

steps.say: One particle sent, one dot. It landed one step right of the middle. Nothing about a single dot looks like a wave.
Three particles, three dots, in three different spots. Where each one lands is random. No one can say in advance.
Ten particles. It still looks like scatter. The emptiest bright spot has even fewer dots than the fullest in-between spot.
Thirty particles. Bright and in-between spots are still level. But watch a spot where the stripe pattern was dark: no dots at all, and its chance is zero.
A thousand particles. Now the bars follow the brightness pattern: tall, half, empty, half, tall. This spread of chances across the screen is the probability distribution.
Each spot's pile is close to the particles sent times its chance. The middle has about a sixth of a thousand, and in-between spots about half that.
Three thousand particles. Each one arrived alone, as one dot. Together they draw interference stripes. This double nature is called wave–particle duality.

understand.explanation: Each particle that goes through the two slits arrives as a single dot in one spot. Where any one dot lands cannot be predicted. What is fixed is the chance: high where the two-slit stripes are bright, half as high in between, and zero in the dark gaps. With a few dots this rule is hidden by randomness, but over hundreds and thousands of dots the counts settle onto the stripe pattern. Experiments have shown this build-up with very faint light (G. I. Taylor, 1909) and with single electrons (Merli, Missiroli and Pozzi, 1974; Frabboni and co-workers, 2012). It has also been seen with atoms and with molecules of up to 2000 atoms. The sources stress that each impact is inherently probabilistic in a way classical physics cannot explain, and what this means is still debated among interpretations of quantum mechanics.
understand.quote: The particle is measured as a single pulse at a single position, while the modulus squared of the wave describes the probability of detecting the particle at a specific place on the screen giving a statistical interference pattern.

The cos² part is the two-slit brightness formula from the double-slit source (s3), with its slit-width factor sinc² left out. The source states that the square of the wave's size gives the probability of detection. In the model, spot k sits where d sinθ/λ = k/4.

concepts.recap: Each particle lands as one random dot, but the chances follow the stripe pattern, so the stripes appear only once many dots pile up.

concepts.title: Ask which slit, and the stripes vanish
concepts.idea: Learning which slit each particle passed through removes the interference term, so the screen shows only the two single-slit patterns added together; partial path information gives partly faded stripes.

predict.question: A new set-up: the slit detector is switched on for every other electron and is fully off for the rest. Afterwards you sort the dots and keep only those from electrons whose slit was NOT checked. What do the dark stripes look like in that sorted pile?
options: Fully dark: the unchecked electrons on their own make crisp stripes
Filled in to a quarter of peak brightness, like the half-checked curve
No stripes at all: having a detector in the room is enough to erase them
Filled in to half brightness, like the every-slit-checked line
why: Right. The stripes fade only because checked electrons land in the smooth spread. Each unchecked electron kept both paths open, so its dots follow the full striped pattern. Sort them out and the stripes come back sharp.

Tempting, because the whole screen does look like the half-checked curve. But that faded look is a blend of two piles: smooth dots from checked electrons and striped dots from unchecked ones. Remove the smooth pile and the blend is gone.

This treats the detector as a curse on the room. What removes the extra term is information about a particle's own path. An electron the detector never touched has no path record, so it still builds stripes.
Half brightness everywhere is what you get when every electron is checked. These electrons were never checked, so nothing removed their interference term.

terms.means: A record of which slit a particle went through, for example from a detector at the slits

model.note: Teaching model: it keeps the earlier assumptions (very narrow slits, single-colour light, a far screen) and ignores the slow fading caused by each slit's own spreading. Each slit alone therefore gives a flat glow at a quarter of peak brightness, which matches source s1: with two equal beams, the maxima are four times as bright as either beam. Three detector settings are drawn side by side: nothing checked, half the particles checked and every particle checked. Path checking is modelled simply. Checked particles add only the smooth two-slit sum, and unchecked ones make full stripes. Real detectors can also give partial information about each particle. Source s3 says this obeys an inequality between visibility and path distinguishability, but gives no formula, so the model does not reproduce it. The spacing rule w = zλ/d is from s3. Other numbers are illustrative.

steps.say: This is the same screen with the same four sliders: colour, slit gap, distance and the marked spot. The solid dark curve is the striped pattern you already know.

New: imagine a detector at the slits that checks which slit a particle used. The lighter curve is the screen when half the particles are checked, and the flat dashed line is the screen when every one is checked.
The wavy dashed line shows how far the striped curve sits above or below that flat line, spot by spot.

goals.text: Find a spot where checking every particle's slit makes the screen as much brighter as possible.
hints: Checking pulls every spot toward the flat dashed line. Which spots sit furthest below it?
Look for a spot where the nothing-checked curve touches zero.
The first such spot is half a stripe spacing from the centre.

Find where the wavy dashed line crosses zero, which is where all three curves meet.
It lies halfway between the centre bright stripe and the first dark stripe.

feedback.correct: Yes. The faded stripes are a blend of two kinds of dots. Checked electrons land in a smooth spread, and unchecked electrons keep both paths open and land in full stripes. Keep only the unchecked ones and you get crisp stripes again.
feedback.incorrect: The fading comes from the checked electrons, not from the room or the detector's mere presence. An electron whose slit was never recorded keeps its interference term, so the dots from unchecked electrons alone still form fully dark stripes.

steps.say: Nobody checks the slits. Each electron lands as one dot, yet thousands of dots pile up into the solid striped curve, the pattern of a wave that passed through both slits.
The flat dashed line is what you would get if each electron simply went through one slit or the other. Each slit alone gives a quarter of peak brightness, so together they give a smooth half.
The wavy dashed line is the gap between those two. Physicists call it the interference term. Where it is positive it adds a bright stripe; where it is negative it carves a dark one.
A record of which slit a particle used is called which-way information. Checked particles lose their interference term, so checking half of them halves it. That gives the lighter, faded curve.
Move to a dark stripe. With nothing checked it is 0%; with half checked it glows at 25%; with every slit checked it is 50%. The dark stripe fills in.
Now a bright stripe: 100%, then 75%, then 50%. What dark stripes gain, bright ones give up. How strongly stripes show is their visibility, and trading it for path information is complementarity.

So each electron alone builds stripes as if it went through both slits, yet the moment you check which slit it used, the interference term is gone and the stripes flatten into the plain sum of two single slits.

understand.explanation: With no detector, the screen shows the two slits' light added together plus an interference term, and that term draws the bright and dark stripes. When a detector records which slit a particle used, that particle loses its interference term and lands in the smooth spread, so the screen becomes the plain sum of two single-slit patterns. Check only some particles and the stripes fade part of the way, with the dark stripes filling in exactly as much as the bright ones dim. The sources describe this through Feynman's thought experiment with detectors at the slits, a Mach–Zehnder version in which blocking or detecting one path removes the interference, and a 1987 experiment that got partial path information without destroying the stripes completely. Two caveats: the simple textbook version cannot be built naively, because detecting a photon absorbs it; and why checking has this effect is still debated (collapse, many worlds, pilot waves), so the sources agree on what is seen but not on what it means.
understand.quote: However, such experiments demonstrate that particles do not form the double-slit interference pattern if one detects which slit they pass through; the pattern instead becomes the sum of two single-slit interference patterns.

check.task: Find a spot away from the centre where checking every particle's slit cuts the brightness in half.
check.hint: Checking pulls every spot toward the flat half-brightness line. Which spots sit furthest above it?
check.misconception: That checking which slit only fills in dark stripes and never dims anything, or that it dims the whole screen. In fact the stripes flatten from both sides toward the smooth sum: bright stripes dim, dark ones brighten, and some spots don't change.

connect.caption: Source s1 gives this without V, the nothing-checked case. I₁ + I₂ is the flat dashed line, the two single slits added. The rest is the interference term, the wavy dashed line. Its phase difference φ₁ − φ₂ changes as you move the marked spot. V is the model's addition, the stripe visibility: V = 1 when nothing is checked, 0.5 when half are checked, and 0 when every slit is checked, leaving only I₁ + I₂.

concepts.recap: Stripes come from an extra term that exists only while both paths stay open. Record the slit and it vanishes, leaving two single slits added; partial records fade the stripes.

activities.prompt: Put the two extremes side by side: the same electrons, slits and screen, with and without a slit detector.

cases.label: No detector: nobody knows the slit
cases.text: Dots pile up into bright and dark stripes. Dark stripes are truly dark, because the interference term cancels the light there completely.

cases.label: Detector checks every particle
cases.text: Each particle is found at one slit. The interference term is gone, and the dots spread smoothly at half brightness: just slit A's pattern plus slit B's.

activities.takeaway: The only difference is whether the path is recorded, and that alone decides whether the interference term exists.
